content: Influenza infection can cause severe health complications in children undergoing cancer treatment. As a result, influenza vaccination is recommended for this population. However, there is uncertainty about how well children with cancer respond to the vaccine while receiving chemotherapy, and the overall benefit of vaccination in this group remains unclear. The primary objectives of this research were to evaluate the ability of the influenza vaccine to stimulate an immune response in children with cancer undergoing chemotherapy, to assess its effectiveness in preventing laboratory-confirmed influenza or influenza-like illnesses, and to identify any adverse effects associated with the vaccine in this population. Comparisons were made with control groups, including those receiving placebo, no intervention, or different vaccine dosage schedules. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to August 2012. Additional sources included reference lists of relevant articles and conference proceedings from organizations such as ICAAC, IDSA, MASCC, and SIOP. The analysis focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled clinical trials (CCTs) that compared the immune and clinical responses to influenza vaccination in children with cancer to those in control groups. A total of 10 studies (1 RCT and 9 CCTs) involving 770 participants were included in the analysis. None of the studies reported clinical outcomes, such as the prevention of influenza or its complications. Instead, all studies focused on immune responses and adverse reactions to the vaccine. Five studies compared immune responses in 272 children undergoing chemotherapy to 166 children who had completed chemotherapy. Four studies compared 236 children receiving chemotherapy to 142 healthy children. Immune responses were measured using criteria such as a four-fold increase in antibody levels, achieving a haemagglutination inhibition (HI) titre greater than 32, and geometric mean titres (GMTs) before and after vaccination. The findings showed that children undergoing chemotherapy had consistently weaker immune responses to the influenza vaccine compared to children who had completed chemotherapy and healthy children. Specifically, the rate of a four-fold rise in antibody levels ranged from 38% to 65% in children receiving chemotherapy, compared to 50% to 86% in those who had completed treatment and 53% to 89% in healthy children. Regarding adverse effects, 391 children with cancer who received the influenza vaccine experienced mild local reactions, such as redness or swelling at the injection site, and low-grade fever. No severe or life-threatening adverse effects were reported. In conclusion, children with cancer undergoing chemotherapy are capable of mounting an immune response to the influenza vaccine. However, the strength of this response is weaker compared to children who are not undergoing chemotherapy. It remains uncertain whether this immune response provides adequate protection against influenza infection or its complications. Further well-designed RCTs are needed to determine the clinical benefits of influenza vaccination in this vulnerable population.
